articles.title: remove.bg Is Shutting Down — Here's a Free, No-Upload Alternative
articles.description: On December 1, 2026 at 9:00 AM CET, remove.bg — the site that turned "one-click background removal"...
articles.body_html:
On December 1, 2026 at 9:00 AM CET, remove.bg — the site that turned "one-click background removal" into an entire category — pulls the plug on its standalone website. It's being folded into Canva, and the API crowd is being pointed toward Leonardo.ai. You can read the notice on remove.bg's own pricing page.

If your workflow just lost its favorite button: don't cry. Your hero is here. It's free, it runs in your browser, and it never uploads your photos.

It's called APIC Web, I built it solo, and this post is the official "shift here" announcement.

What's actually happening to remove.bg?

Quick recap, because a lot of people are about to find out the hard way:

  • The standalone site dies on Dec 1, 2026. Bookmarks, muscle memory, that one tab you always keep open — gone.
  • Background removal moves into Canva, where it's a Pro-tier feature, not a free utility.
  • Free was never really free. remove.bg's free tier only ever gave you preview-resolution downloads. Full-resolution cut-outs cost credits — roughly $9/month for 40 images.
  • API users are being migrated to Leonardo.ai's pricing.

So the real question trending right now is: "What's the best free remove.bg alternative that gives full-resolution transparent PNGs without a subscription?"

That's literally the question I built APIC to answer.

Meet APIC Web — the free background remover that never uploads your photos

👉 https://apic-app.vercel.app/

APIC Web is a free online photo editor and AI background remover that runs 100% on your device, inside your browser tab. The AI models are compiled to WebAssembly, downloaded once, cached, and executed locally. Your images are never sent to any server. Not for processing, not for "quality improvement", not for anything.

And the part that matters most for everyone migrating off remove.bg:

  • ✅ Full-resolution output — not a preview thumbnail
  • ✅ Transparent PNG / WebP with edge refinement and color-fringe removal
  • ✅ No credits, no watermarks, no paid tiers — there is no pricing page because there is no price
  • ✅ No account required — for anything. Editing, AI tools, exporting, even batch ZIP downloads all work signed-out. There's an optional one-tap Google sign-in if you want to join the community counter — if you don't, just ignore it. Sign-in is a community feature, not a gate.

APIC vs remove.bg vs Canva: the honest comparison

APIC Web remove.bg (until Dec 1) Canva BG Remover
Price $0, forever Free previews; ~$9/mo for 40 full-res credits Pro subscription
Full-res free downloads ✅ Unlimited ❌ Credits only ❌ Pro only
Photo uploads to a server Never — on-device AI Every image Every image
Account needed No (optional) Yes Yes
Bulk / batch removal ✅ Free Batch Studio → ZIP Paid API Pro feature
Works offline ✅ Free Windows app ❌ ❌

Why "no upload" isn't a gimmick — it's the architecture

Here's the dev-to-dev explanation of why APIC can be genuinely free while everyone else meters credits:

Cloud editors pay for GPU compute every time you click "remove background". That's why they ration you — credits, queues, paywalls. Their free tier is a funnel.

APIC flips the model: your device is the GPU. The segmentation and inpainting models run in your browser via WebAssembly. My per-image compute cost is exactly ₹0.00, so "free forever" isn't a marketing promise — it's a property of the architecture.

It also means APIC is the rare background remover you can safely use on ID scans, client work under NDA, unreleased product photos, or anything you'd never paste into someone else's server.

Three engines, picked for your hardware

Mode First download Built for
Light ~5 MB Phones
Fast ~44 MB Everyday use, any device
Maximum ~176 MB Multi-pass accuracy, PC recommended

Models download once and are cached — repeat runs start fast. If a download fails, APIC retries automatically. Every AI result can be undone with Ctrl+Z.

Plot twist: it's not just a background remover

remove.bg did one thing. APIC is a full studio. Same tab, same zero-upload promise:

  • 🧽 Remove Object — paint over anything and an on-device inpainting model fills it in, color-matched and re-grained to your photo. Ultra mode uses LaMa (a large Fourier-convolution inpainting network, ~208 MB) for big/complex objects; Best/Fast use the lighter MI-GAN (~28 MB) that works on phones. If a model can't load, it degrades gracefully: Ultra → MI-GAN → quick patch fill.
  • 🔍 AI Upscale 2× / 4× — Real-ESRGAN (x4plus for max accuracy, a 5 MB fast model for phones).
  • 🎨 Pro color suite — live histogram, RGB curves, an 8-band HSL mixer, 3-way color grading, white balance, tone and detail controls.
  • 🎬 Export your grade as a .cube LUT — a real 33×33×33 3D LUT you can drop into DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, or Photoshop. Grade a still, carry the look into your video timeline. (Color-only operations are baked in; spatial effects like grain and vignette aren't, because they're not color transforms.) I haven't seen another browser tool do this.
  • 🔁 Convert — PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, ICO, PDF, even PSD with layers kept.
  • 🗜️ Compress to a target file size — tell it "300 KB" and it searches quality levels for the best-looking image that fits. No guessing.
  • 📐 Resize — exact pixels or percent, with step-down (multi-pass halving) resampling so shrinks stay crisp instead of muddy.
  • 📦 Batch Studio — drop in many images, remove backgrounds / resize / compress / convert them all, download one ZIP. Free, on-device, no account.
  • 📱 Social presets — exact-size profiles, banners, posts and stories for 15 networks (Instagram, YouTube, X, TikTok, LinkedIn, Discord, Twitch, Spotify…), with safe-zone guides and automatic platform size limits. Export one size or a ZIP of all of them.
  • ✨ One-click extras — auto-enhance, smart crop, fit subject, crop to subject.

Prefer offline? There's a Windows app

Download APIC for PC — fully offline, same edit/convert/compress stack, no account needed to download or use it.

FAQ (the stuff you're about to Google)

What is the best free remove.bg alternative in 2026?

If you want full-resolution cut-outs with no credits and no uploads: APIC Web. It runs on-device AI in your browser and stays free because there's no server compute to pay for.

Is APIC Web really free? What's the catch?

No paid tiers, no credits, no watermarks. The "catch" is that your own device does the work — which is also the privacy feature.

Do I need to sign up to remove a background or export?

No. Everything works without an account, including exports and batch downloads. Google sign-in is optional — it exists for the community counter and update emails. Skip it freely.

Are my photos uploaded anywhere?

Never. The only network traffic is the one-time model download from a CDN. Your images stay in your browser's memory, on your machine.

Does it work on phones?

Yes — the Light engine is a ~5 MB model made for phones, and MI-GAN object removal works on mobile too.

Can I remove backgrounds from many images at once?

Yes. Batch Studio processes a whole pile locally and hands you one ZIP. Free, no sign-in.

Bookmark it before December 1

The remove.bg shutdown is going to strand a lot of people in three weeks. If this post found you before that happens — you're early, not late.

🔗 apic-app.vercel.app — open it, drop an image, hit Remove background. That's the whole onboarding.

I'm a solo developer, and APIC is a product of Akhouri Systems. If it saves your workflow, do me one favor: share it with someone who's still mourning remove.bg. And if you want a feature, comment — I read everything.

Built with WebAssembly, stubbornness, and an HP 240 G9(my bro).
— Akhouri Anmol Kumar, Akhouri Systems

articles.title: Scope WebMCP Tools to the Open React Workflow
articles.description: On the Events list, the browser discovered zero WebMCP tools. Opening an event draft exposed four....
articles.body_html:
On the Events list, the browser discovered zero WebMCP tools. Opening an event draft exposed four. Switching to a trip draft replaced them with five trip tools.

That route sequence is the behavior I wanted when Trip Workbench gained a second workflow. Registering every operation at startup would have exposed two unrelated domains even when only one editor was visible.

Page-scoped tools make the current context clearer. They also create a design question: how does an agent enter a workflow whose tools exist only after the right page is open?

Keep domain identity in the contract

The event editor has a title, date range, time zone, location mode, location label, and notes. The trip editor has airports, travel dates, cabin, traveler count, and purpose.

Both workflows reuse authorization, revision, and command-receipt patterns, but they keep separate coordinators, services, tables, validation rules, policy versions, and identifiers. Event tools accept eventId; trip tools accept draftId.

The event editor exposes:

Tool Purpose
get_event_draft Read saved fields, revision, status, and unsaved-change state
update_event_draft Apply an allowed patch to an expected revision
validate_event_draft Return field issues and policy findings
prepare_event_review Show findings while the event remains a draft

This synthetic example does not send invitations, connect to calendars, or book venues.

Register when the editor has context

The React editor registers tools only after it has a draft identity and status. A condensed lifecycle looks like this:

useEffect(() => {
  if (!eventId || draftStatus !== "draft") return;

  const registration = new AbortController();

  registerEventDraftTools({
    eventId,
    canMutate: Boolean(canMutate),
    coordinator: eventCoordinator,
    signal: registration.signal,
    onStatus: setRegistration,
  });

  return () => registration.abort();
}, [eventId, draftStatus, canMutate, eventCoordinator]);

Chrome’s current imperative API documents this signal-based lifecycle. As of Chrome 153, aborting the registration removes the tool without cancelling an already-running execution. That is helpful for component cleanup, but it means route cleanup and in-flight operation safety are separate responsibilities.

The draft identity belongs in the dependency list. React may retain the same component type while moving from one event to another; the old tools must disappear and the new handlers must bind to the new event.

Test the exact route sequence

The native browser run signed in normally, used visible navigation, created a synthetic event draft, and inspected the browser’s real tool collection. It did not call the coordinator directly.

Context Discovered interface
Traveler on Trips list none
Traveler on Events list none
Traveler editing an event four event tools
Traveler editing a trip five trip tools
Traveler back on Events list none
Traveler reopening the event four event tools
Observer editing the event read, validate, prepare
Observer back on Events list none

An exact-name assertion catches stale registrations:

const expected = [
  "get_event_draft",
  "prepare_event_review",
  "update_event_draft",
  "validate_event_draft",
];

const actual = page.webmcp.tools()
  .map((tool) => tool.name)
  .sort();

assert.deepEqual(actual, expected);

The observer result is useful but limited. Omitting a mutation tool reduces accidental exposure; it does not authorize anything. The server must still reject writes from an actor without permission.

Execute a useful operation, not just discovery

Tool names alone do not prove that the page contract works. The run updated a synthetic workshop, validated it, and prepared an inline review.

{
  "title": "Customer engineering workshop",
  "startDate": "2026-11-25",
  "endDate": "2026-11-26",
  "timeZone": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "locationMode": "manual",
  "locationLabel": "Demo workshop room",
  "notes": "Synthetic example; no invitations"
}

The accepted update moved the draft from revision 1 to 2. prepare_event_review displayed a MANUAL_LOCATION requirement with canSubmit: true and submitted: false. The visible title matched an independent database query, and the event remained a draft with zero submissions.

The injected test clock was October 14, 2026, so the dates were still in the future. Pinning time matters when validation depends on dates.

A narrow interface needs a way in

The Events list intentionally exposes no editor tools, so those tools cannot open their own workflow.

The recorded run used the normal Events link and “New event draft” button. A browser agent with navigation and actuation can take a similar path. A client limited to WebMCP calls cannot.

There are two defensible designs:

  1. Treat browser navigation as part of the client contract.
  2. Add a bounded list-level tool to open an authorized draft or create a new one.

I would avoid a generic “call any API” or “run arbitrary JavaScript” escape hatch. It destroys the narrow schemas and server checks that make the editor tools reviewable.

Do not turn tool count into a performance claim

This run proves that the discovered interface changes with route and role. It does not prove that a model completes tasks faster with four tools than with nine.

That requires a separate evaluation: keep the task and executable behavior fixed, vary the visible tool set, and measure wrong-target updates, workflow-entry failures, correct persisted outcomes, recovery steps, and final-answer accuracy.

The current evidence supports a narrower conclusion: expose editing tools where the relevant object is visible, remove them when the context ends, preserve server authorization, and design an explicit entry path for the clients you actually support.

articles.title: Build an Offline AI Study App with Local Models (Liquid AI LFM3-1.7B)
articles.description: I ran Liquid AI's LFM3-1.7B in the browser with WebGPU and built Grading Buddy, an offline study app that answers only from notes I've checked.
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone. Today I want to show you how you can use local models, using Liquid AI's LFM3, their latest model.

What local models are

First of all, what does a local model mean? It means a model that is on your device. You download it, and it runs on your device. So you don't need a connection to the internet, you don't need to spend any money because it's free and on your device, and everything stays private. There are a lot of benefits to using local models.

A minimal LFM3 chat in the browser

Let me show you a very simple example. I built a very small chat app, about 45 lines of code, just to show how easily you can get started. I'm getting Transformers.js from Hugging Face, then there's my model, and I'm using WebGPU so it runs in the browser. That's basically all you need to build something like this. I told you it was minimal.

Then you ask your question: what is the capital of France? It downloads the model, the model is now running on my device, it's not going to the cloud and it's not costing me any money. The capital of France is Paris. I can change that to Ireland, and I get Dublin, really fast.

The tech, in plain words

Before we go further, here's what's actually going on in that tiny page.

  • LFM3-1.7B is Liquid AI's small text model in the LFM3 family. Small enough to run on a laptop, and good at following "answer only from these facts" instructions. I use the ONNX export on Hugging Face, which is the version made to run in a browser. You can read more on the model card and in Liquid's docs.
  • Transformers.js is Hugging Face's JavaScript library for running models in the browser. It downloads the model and runs it for you, so you don't need a server.
  • WebGPU is the browser API that lets a web page use your computer's graphics card. A model does a lot of maths, and the GPU does it much faster than the CPU. That's why the app needs a desktop browser with WebGPU, like Chrome or Edge.

Loading the model

This is the heart of the minimal page. One import, one pipeline, then you ask it a question:

import { pipeline } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@huggingface/transformers@4.3.2";

const chat = await pipeline("text-generation", "onnx-community/LFM3-1.7B-ONNX", {
  dtype: "q4f16",
  device: "webgpu",
});

const out = await chat(
  [
    { role: "system", content: "You are a helpful assistant. Answer briefly." },
    { role: "user", content: "What is the capital of France?" },
  ],
  { max_new_tokens: 150, do_sample: false, tokenizer_encode_kwargs: { enable_thinking: false } },
);

q4f16 is a compressed version of the model, which keeps the download to about 1.1 GB. device: "webgpu" runs it on the GPU. enable_thinking: false turns off LFM3's thinking so you get a direct answer. The whole page is in examples/minimal in the repo.

What gets downloaded and cached

The first time you press Download and start, the browser fetches the model files from Hugging Face, about 1.1 GB, just once. Transformers.js keeps them in the browser's cache, and in the full app (more on that below) a service worker caches the app itself. So after that first download it works with no internet at all.

How the app works

The full app wraps the model in a few simple steps:

  1. Topic match. It picks the grading topic that best fits your question.
  2. Say no early. If nothing matches, the app tells you it's not part of the grading and doesn't call the model at all.
  3. Give the model the notes. LFM3 gets that topic's facts and answers in a sentence or two.
  4. Check the answer. A grounding check (Korean terms, numbers, type of answer) and a required-facts check both have to pass.
  5. Fall back to the note. If either check fails, you see the note card labelled From the notes instead.

The model runs in a Web Worker so the page doesn't freeze while it thinks. Liquid's own docs say "Use retrieval or search for knowledge-heavy tasks", and that's exactly why the facts come from my notes and not from the model's memory.

Where a small model falls short

Now, what if I ask what Chon-Ji means? I'm studying for my Taekwon-Do grading, so that's a real question for me. It told me Chon-Ji is a Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan. No, it's not. Chon-Ji means heaven and earth.

And when I asked what the tenets of Taekwon-Do are, it didn't give me the answer.

That's the problem with local models. Sometimes they don't have enough knowledge, and you think, right, this is not good enough, I need a bigger model and I'll just pay for it. But no. You can use local models in so many other ways.

Giving the model your own notes

So the minimal version proved the model runs on my device, fast and for free. It just didn't know Taekwon-Do. And that's what I actually needed help with for my grading. So I went and built a proper app around it, called Grading Buddy. It's a study app that only answers from notes I've checked, and tells you when something isn't part of the grading.

I could have fine-tuned the model and shown it more Taekwon-Do. Instead, what I'm doing is giving it a content.json file with extra content about Taekwon-Do. It's the same content I use on the website to show that information. Then the chat part lets students ask their questions about Taekwon-Do and get the correct answers.

Grading Buddy: Ask, answered on device

So this is the app, Grading Buddy, with everything about Chon-Ji, the belts, the tenets and the rest. If I ask "what are the five tenets?", I get courtesy, integrity, perseverance, self-control and indomitable spirit. That answer was written by LFM3 on this device.

I can also see how it was answered. That's built in for this demo, and you wouldn't want it in the real app. But you can see the path, that it used the model, how long it took, and the checks it needed to pass to get to that answer.

When an answer check fails

Next I asked how many moves are in Chon-Ji. It thought about it, and then it couldn't answer. So what happened? The panel shows it failed on a missing required fact. So we can look in our notes, the JSON file, and find out why that check failed and which notes are missing. Then, rather than fine-tuning the model, we fine-tune the notes so it can get the answer to that question.

Then I asked how to count to ten in Korean, and that answer came from the model on this device too. And when I asked my first question again, what does Chon-Ji mean, I got heaven and earth, the first pattern you learn.

So that's how you can use a local model in your app to do some really fun things. People type their questions and get answers based on the knowledge you give it.

Quiz and Learn why

You can do some extra fun things too. In the quiz, one question was which part of the foot you use for a front snap kick. I put the heel, which is totally wrong. It's the ball of the foot. That feedback comes straight from the notes, in simple words. But you can also click Learn why, and the explanation is a little bit nicer: a front snap kick is called apcha busigi, you lift the knee, and it's a strong kick to the front. Just some extra wording in there, and I quite like it.

That could be really nice when you're helping children learn. The model can make your answers a little more fun and friendly. On another question, the Learn why explanation walked through the end of the pattern, steps 17, 18 and 19, and bringing the left foot back to parallel stance. That's really helpful, and much nicer than just saying yes, it's right.

Try it yourself

So that's what you can do with local models. That's Liquid AI's LFM3, and I've made the app open source, so go and check it out, download it and play around with it. The README is very simple: git clone, cd into the folder, npm ci, npm run dev, then ask those questions and build something yourself. Check out the minimal file too if you want to. Local models are very cool and worth trying out. So go build something cool, and have fun.

  • Grading Buddy repo
  • Live app (desktop browser with WebGPU)
  • LFM3-1.7B on Hugging Face
  • Transformers.js
  • Liquid AI

articles.title: Composio vs Nango vs Scalekit: What Changes When Your Agent Goes to Production
articles.description: The demo passed. The security review didn't.   Here's a story you've probably lived, or will...
articles.body_html:
The demo passed. The security review didn't.

Here's a story you've probably lived, or will soon.

A team at Brightwater Logistics builds an agent that reads a customer's Xero invoices, checks usage in Amplitude, and drafts renewal outreach in Apollo. They wire it up with an integration platform in a weekend. The demo is great. Sales signs the first enterprise customer.

Then the customer's security team sends a questionnaire, and the questions are different from anything the demo answered:

  • Where do our users' tokens live, and are they kept apart from your other customers' tokens?
  • Can your agent do anything our users didn't authorize? What stops it?
  • Our Snowflake access uses RSA key pairs and our Google Workspace uses domain-wide delegation. Do you support those?
  • If something goes wrong, can you show us which agent did what, for which user, under which permission?
  • Our data can't leave our cloud. Can this run inside our VPC?

None of those are about whether a connector exists. All of them are about what happens after the agent is connected.

That's the gap this article covers. I'm comparing three platforms teams often weigh at this stage: Composio, Nango and Scalekit. Each one is judged on the questions above.

What each one does well

Before the hard questions, credit where it's due.

Composio has the biggest catalog of the three. Its toolkits page lists 1,742 toolkits. With managed auth, Composio registers the OAuth apps for popular toolkits like GitHub, Gmail and Slack, so you can get to a first tool call without registering anything yourself. Nothing here gets you to a working demo faster.

Nango lets you own the integration code. Its functions are TypeScript you write, version and deploy, and it supports 700+ APIs for auth. You can self-host it: a free version covers auth and the proxy, and the Enterprise version adds tool calls, syncs and the MCP server on your own Kubernetes or in your own cloud account.

Scalekit is built for the stage after the demo. Its docs list 600+ connectors and 30,000+ tools. It's built around per-user connected accounts, scoped tool bundles, and per-call logs, and it can run in your own infrastructure.

The question changed

In 2025, the question was: does a connector exist for the app I need?

In 2026, the question is: what is the agent allowed to do once it's connected?

Connectors are close to a commodity now. All three platforms cover Apollo and Xero, for example. What differs is everything around the connector: who holds the credentials, what stops a bad call, and what you can prove afterwards.

You can build that layer yourself. It's a token vault per user, refresh logic, a proxy that adds tokens at call time, a permission check in front of every tool, a log pipeline, and a deployment you can ship into a customer's cloud. Each piece is a few weeks of work, and every new app and customer adds to it. So the real choice is which platform takes over which pieces, and which ones you keep.

Six questions enterprise customers ask

1. Where do the credentials live, and who else's are next to them?

All three encrypt tokens at rest. The differences are in who holds them and what separates one customer from another.

  • Composio stores and refreshes connected-account credentials for you, whether you use its managed OAuth apps or your own. That makes its infrastructure part of your recovery path. Its own disclosure of the May 2026 incident reported leaked connected-account tokens for about 0.3% of active connections, mostly GitHub and Gmail. Composio says its APIs no longer return those tokens. The lesson applies to every vendor in this space: wherever tokens are pooled, that's your blast radius.
  • Nango encrypts credentials with AES-256-GCM, with keys wrapped in AWS KMS. Its security page describes isolation at the environment level: each environment has separate credentials, connections and API keys. For production it expects your own OAuth apps.
  • Scalekit encrypts every token and API key with a key unique to your environment, wrapped by a master key in Google Cloud KMS that's kept apart from the database (overview). You can bring your own OAuth apps, so consent screens show your brand and rate limits are yours.

None of the three docs describe a separate vault per end customer. If a customer needs that, separate environments or a self-hosted deployment are the way to get it, on any of them.

2. Can the agent do more than the user authorized?

A valid token proves who the user is. It doesn't stop a prompt-injected email from asking the agent to delete a record.

  • Composio limits a session to the toolkits you pass, can block tools by hint such as destructiveHint, and can pause a call for the user's approval. Approvals are labeled experimental.
  • Nango gives each agent session a toolset with allow and deny lists. Beyond that, authorization is code you write into each integration function. A session's scope is fixed once it's created and lasts up to 15 days by default. The docs also note that turning on the nango_proxy tool lets the agent reach any endpoint of a connected integration.
  • Scalekit puts each agent role behind a Virtual MCP server that lists exactly which tools it can call, and you mint a short-lived session token per user before each run. A token minted as read-only can't call write tools. The connected account only holds the scopes the user approved, so the app itself still refuses anything the user can't do.

3. How deep do the connectors go beyond popular apps?

Catalog size is one number. Depth on the apps your customers actually use is another. Here's Apollo, an app sales agents rely on:

  • Composio: 67 tools, with API key auth.
  • Nango: 26 tools and 6 syncs, and you can write more.
  • Scalekit: 75 tools, 2 of them marked destructive, with both OAuth and API key versions of the connector.

All three also have Xero. For Amplitude, Nango and Scalekit list connectors; I didn't find one on Composio's toolkit pages, so check before you rely on it.

4. What about auth that isn't OAuth?

Enterprise systems often don't use OAuth at all. Snowflake recommends RSA key pairs. Google Workspace admins use domain-wide delegation. Data platforms use service accounts.

  • Composio lists OAUTH2, API_KEY, BEARER_TOKEN and BASIC as auth schemes in its glossary.
  • Nango lists OAuth 2.0, OAuth 1.0a, API keys, basic auth and custom auth, and some integrations have a client-credentials version (Xero, for example).
  • Scalekit's connector list includes Snowflake with RSA key pairs, BigQuery with a service account, Google Workspace with domain-wide delegation, and Databricks with client credentials.

If your customer runs Azure AD service accounts, ask each vendor directly. I couldn't confirm that pattern in any of the three docs.

5. Can you prove which agent did what, for which user?

  • Composio keeps execution logs for up to a year on every plan. Request arguments and responses are stored by default; zero data retention keeps metadata only.
  • Nango keeps logs for 15 days on Nango Cloud, exportable through OpenTelemetry, plus an audit trail kept a year and exportable as CSV.
  • Scalekit logs every tool call with the agent, tool, user, duration and result, and marks failures as connector or API errors. It records metadata, not content. Logs are kept 30 days on Free and Growth; longer retention and SIEM streaming are Enterprise features.

6. Can it run where the customer's data has to stay?

  • Composio lists self-hosting as an enterprise feature.
  • Nango offers free self-hosting for auth and the proxy, and Enterprise BYOC or self-managed deployments on AWS, GCP, Azure or on-prem Kubernetes with the full feature set.
  • Scalekit runs self-hosted on your Kubernetes cluster with an enterprise license, and its docs list air-gapped environments as a reason to do it. The managed service has separate US and EU deployments.

Side by side

Composio Nango Scalekit
Catalog 1,742 toolkits 700+ APIs for auth 600+ connectors, 30,000+ tools
Credentials Held and refreshed by Composio AES-256-GCM, isolated per environment Key per environment, wrapped in Cloud KMS; your own OAuth apps
Limits on the agent Toolkits, tool hints, approvals (experimental) Allow and deny lists; your function code Virtual MCP server per role, per-user session token, read-only tokens
Apollo depth 67 tools 26 tools, 6 syncs 75 tools
Beyond OAuth API key, bearer, basic OAuth 1.0a, API key, basic, custom RSA key pairs, service accounts, domain-wide delegation, client credentials
Logs Up to 1 year, payloads stored by default 15 days, OpenTelemetry export, 1-year audit trail Every call, connector vs API errors; 30 days, SIEM on Enterprise
Self-hosting Enterprise Free (auth and proxy) or Enterprise Enterprise, including air-gapped

Want the same comparison on video? Here's Scalekit's walkthrough of Composio vs Scalekit:

Which one fits your stage

There's no single winner here. It depends on where you are.

  • You need a working demo this week: Composio. The catalog is huge and managed auth gets you to a first tool call quickly.
  • You want to write and own every integration: Nango. The code is yours, and you can self-host it.
  • You're shipping to enterprise customers: Scalekit. Scoped tools per agent role, a session per user, auth beyond OAuth, per-call logs, and a self-hosted option are the things their security reviews ask about.

Teams also move between stages. If you started on Composio and the security questions are arriving now, Scalekit has a migration guide. One thing to plan for: OAuth refresh tokens are tied to the OAuth client that issued them, so each user connects once more after the move.

When you don't need any of them

If your agent runs for one person, on that person's own API keys, against two or three apps, you don't need an integration platform yet. Keep the keys in environment variables and ship. The calculation changes when the second customer connects their own accounts, or when the first security questionnaire arrives.

Voice agents raise the stakes again: there's no screen for an OAuth consent mid-call, and every extra tool slows the spoken reply. Give Your Voice Agent Hands walks through a sales voice agent that updates HubSpot, Apollo, Google Calendar and Gmail after a call.

Getting started

To try per-user tool calls with your own accounts, start with the Scalekit quickstart.

articles.title: How to Scroll Between Separate Components in React
articles.description: Let's say you're creating a reusable button component in React and want to use it to navigate to a...
articles.body_html:
Let's say you're creating a reusable button component in React and want to use it to navigate to a particular section or component of your website from various other components.

One approach we're familiar with is using <Link /> and <Route />. However, these are primarily used for navigation between different routes. What if you want to scroll to a specific section within the same page instead?
That's where this blog comes in! You'll learn how to scroll between separate components in React.

First, let's create a Button component. 

export default function Button() {
    return (
        <button>Scroll to View</button>
    );
}

Next, let's create the section/component we want to scroll to.

export default function CatGallery() {
    return (
        <div>
            <h2>Hey there, Hooman!</h2>
            <img
                src="https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1592194996308-7b43878e84a6?q=80&w=687&auto=format&fit=crop&ixlib=rb-4.1.0&ixid=NHwxMjA3fDA%3D"
                alt="orange cat"
            />
        </div>
    );
}

Now, we have two separate components and our task is to scroll to CatGallery when the user clicks the button component.

But how do we do that?

As we know, in React, every component is like an isolated island. The Button component only knows about itself and CatGallery only knows about itself.

Finding the Common Ancestor

Remember how Harry and Voldemort shared a common ancestor in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows? Well, we need to find a common ancestor here too!

To connect two separate components, we need to move up the component tree and find their lowest common parent.

Let's create our App.jsx:

import {useRef} from "react";
import Hero from './Hero';
import CatGallery from './CatGallery';

export default function App() {
    const galleryRef = useRef(null);

    return (
        <div>
            <Hero /> // This is where you place your Button component
            <CatGallery /> // This is the target section
        </div>
    );
}

export default App;

Centralizing Control

Now comes the interesting part!

We'll create the useRef hook and the scroll function inside this common parent component.

Since App renders both Hero (which contains the Button) and CatGallery, it acts as the middleman connecting the trigger (the button click) to the target (the CatGallery section).

This way, both components can communicate through their common parent without needing to know about each other's internal implementation.

So, how exactly does this work?

useRef creates a persistent object ({ current: null }) that survives across component re-renders. Unlike state, changing its current property does not trigger a re-render.

Attaching the ref to the DOM:

When you pass this ref down to CatGallery and attach it to an actual HTML element (such as <div ref={ref}>), React automatically assigns that DOM element to galleryRef.current once the component mounts.

export default function CatGallery({ ref }) {
    return (
        <div ref={ref}>
            <h2>Hey there, Hooman!</h2>
            <img
                src="https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1592194996308-7b43878e84a6?q=80&w=687&auto=format&fit=crop&ixlib=rb-4.1.0&ixid=NHwxMjA3fDA%3D"
                alt="orange cat"
            />
        </div>
    );
}

Scrolling to the target:

Calling galleryRef.current.scrollIntoView() tells the browser to scroll the viewport until the referenced DOM element becomes visible. By passing { behavior: "smooth" }, we make the scrolling animation smooth rather than instant.

import { useRef } from "react";
import Hero from "./Hero";
import CatGallery from "./CatGallery";

export default function App() {
    const galleryRef = useRef(null);

    const handleScrollToExplore = () => {
        galleryRef.current?.scrollIntoView({
            behavior: "smooth"
        });
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <Hero onClick={handleScrollToExplore} />
            {/* This is where you place your Button component */}

            <CatGallery ref={galleryRef} />
            {/* This is the target section */}
        </div>
    );
}

export default App;

The Trigger (Prop Drilling + Callback Functions)

In JavaScript, functions are first-class citizens. This means they can be passed around just like strings, numbers, or other values.

App passes the handleScrollToExplore function down to Hero through props, and Hero passes it further down to Button.

export default function Hero({ onClick }) {
    return (
        <main>
            <h1>Hey there, nice to have you!</h1>
            <Button goToExplore={onClick} />
        </main>
    );
}

The Button component doesn't need to know where it's scrolling or how the scrolling works. It simply needs to call the function it receives (goToExplore) whenever a user clicks the button.

export default function Button({ goToExplore }) {
    return (
        <button onClick={goToExplore}>
            Scroll to View
        </button>
    );
}

This is the beauty of callback functions! They allow one component to trigger an action without needing to know the internal logic behind it.
