articles.body_html:
The word landed in the middle of a Tuesday meeting, in the big room, the one where the air conditioner hummed like it was thinking about quitting.

We were redesigning the sync service, and the lead said, "We'll go with eventual consistency on this one," and kept talking like he had just said something normal, like "we'll use Postgres" or "let's order lunch." Everyone around the table made small agreeing noises. I made one too. Then I nodded.

I had a whole technique for the nod by then, though I didn't know it yet. It was slow, two beats, chin down and up, with a little pen tap at the end, as if the nod had a full stop. It said: yes, of course, eventual consistency, the obvious choice, carry on. It said all of that in half a second, and none of it was true. I had no idea what eventual consistency was. I had heard the words before, the way you hear a song on the radio and can hum the chorus but not name the band. Consistency. Eventually. Something about databases agreeing with each other, probably. Eventually.

The meeting moved on. I wrote the words in my notebook and put a star next to them, the way you star a message you plan to read later and never do.

Afterwards, back at my desk, I googled it: "eventual consistency simple explanation." The first result was a blog post with a diagram of two databases holding hands. The second was a Wikipedia page that used the word "convergence" in the first sentence and lost me by the third. The third was a forum answer that began, "Actually, it's quite simple," and then ran for nine hundred words. I read all three. I closed all three. I understood it the way you understand a joke someone explains to you: the words went in, the meaning waved at me from a distance and kept walking.

So I did what I always did. I nodded harder.

That is the part nobody tells you about the nod. It works. That is the problem. Nobody checks. Meetings move fast, and a confident nod is a tiny green light. The lead saw mine and kept going. The next week, someone said "idempotency" and I nodded at that too, and wrote it in the notebook with another star. The week after that it was "backpressure." By March the notebook had eleven stars. Eleven words I had nodded at and never looked up. My notebook started to look like a star chart. I told myself I would look them all up on Friday. I never looked them up on Friday. Friday was for the things I had already put off on Thursday.

I started rehearsing explanations in the shower. That was the lowest point, probably, though I didn't know it then. I would stand there with the water going cold and explain eventual consistency to the tiles, in a confident voice, using words like "convergence" that I had stolen from the Wikipedia page. The tiles were a generous audience. They never asked follow-up questions.

The dread came later, and it came in a specific shape. It was not the fear of being found out in general. It was the fear of one sentence: "Salam, what do you think?" The lead said it the way leads do, casually, eyes scanning the room for someone who had been quiet. I had been quiet because I was busy nodding. I started volunteering to take the meeting notes, because a man writing things down has a reason to look at his notebook instead of at the lead. My notes were excellent. My notes were the best notes in the team. They were also a hiding place with bullet points.

Once, I nearly asked. The lead said "backpressure" and I actually opened my mouth, and then a senior engineer asked a question about the queue depth, a real question with numbers in it, and the moment closed like a door. I told myself the timing was wrong. The timing was always wrong.

The worst part was that I was not stupid. I knew that, in the way you know things at 2 a.m. and forget by 10. I could build the thing. I could read the code. I just could not say the words out loud without feeling like someone would ask me to keep going, and then I would be standing there with an empty bucket and a long way to the well. So I kept the bucket hidden and nodded.

Then, one Thursday, the bucket came out anyway.

It was a sprint review. The product manager asked whether users would see their updates straight away, and I heard myself say, "It's eventually consistent, so, you know, a few seconds, max." I said it the way I had heard other people say it: lightly, confidently, like a man describing his own kitchen. And then Maya, the senior dev, who was refilling her water bottle by the window, said, "Eventually doesn't have a max. That's the whole deal. It could be a second. It could be an hour, if something's stuck. Eventually is a promise without a deadline."

She said it the way you tell someone the lift is out of order. No smile of victory, no pause for the room to enjoy it. She just said it, and sat down, and the meeting went on. Nobody laughed. Nobody even looked at me the way I had spent a year imagining people would look at me. The product manager said "ah, okay, good to know," and wrote something down. The floor did not open. The sky did not fall. I sat there with my face burning and a strange feeling underneath the burning, like the moment after you take a plaster off and find the skin underneath is fine.

That evening I looked it up properly. Not the frantic googling of before. I read one article slowly, with the notebook open, and I wrote down what it meant in my own words, the way you would explain it to a friend: the system promises the copies will agree, but it does not promise when. I wrote that sentence twice. Then I looked up idempotency, and backpressure, and three other stars. It took forty minutes. Forty minutes, for a year of dread. I did the maths on that and decided not to do the maths on that. Then I closed the laptop and went for a walk, and I felt something I had not felt in a year of meetings. I felt like I had put down a bag I had forgotten I was carrying.

The next week, the lead said "idempotency" again. I heard myself say, "Sorry — quick one. When you say idempotent, you mean we can run the same request twice and nothing bad happens, right?"

The room did something I did not expect. Two people visibly relaxed, the way people relax when someone else says the thing they were thinking. One of them laughed and said, "Thank god. I was going to google that tonight." And Maya, from her corner, said, "I have a bookmark folder for this stuff. I look it up every single time. Eleven years in, and I still check."

Eleven years. She had been doing this eleven years, and she still checked. I thought about my notebook full of stars. I thought about the hiding place with bullet points. I almost laughed, right there in the meeting, and I had to turn it into a cough.

After that, the questions got easier, the way anything gets easier once you have done it once and survived. I asked about backpressure. I asked about the retry policy. Once I asked a question and the answer was something I actually knew, and I felt foolish for about four seconds, and then I forgot about it, because nobody else remembered it either. I asked a question in a meeting with the client, and the client said, "Good question, I was wondering that too," and I wrote that down in the notebook as well, without a star, because some things you do not need to look up later.

A year later, almost to the week, I was in the same big room, the same air conditioner still thinking about quitting, and the lead said "eventual consistency" again. This time I was the one who had been in the room the longest. And across the table, a new engineer, first week, did the nod. The slow nod. Two beats. Chin down and up. And then the pen tap, the little full stop. I knew that nod the way you know your own handwriting. I still have the notebook. The stars are still there.

After the meeting I caught him by the kettle. "Hey," I said. "Eventual consistency. It just means the copies promise to agree, but nobody promises when. That's all it is."

He looked at me, and his shoulders did something I recognised. They went down, half an inch, like he had put down a bag.

"Oh," he said. "That's it?"

"That's it," I said.

He nodded. And so did I. This time I knew what I was nodding at.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: One Month After the Hackathon: Why My 4-Service App Stopped Working (and What @mansio Caught in the Verifiers)
articles.description: What breaks a month after a hackathon, and what a fellow DEV writer caught in the verifiers.   TL;DR:...
articles.body_html:
What breaks a month after a hackathon, and what a fellow DEV writer caught in the verifiers.

TL;DR: A month after shipping README Clew 2, I opened it up and every scan failed. Nothing was wrong with the deterministic verifiers or with Jev on Glasser. Instead, three small operational traps lined up at once: an expired 30-day GitHub token on a tool that only reads public repos, a rotated Claude Haiku key scoped only to Development in Vercel, and a substring bug that fellow DEV writer Mikhail (@mansio) found and fixed in PR #2.

In October I built README Clew 2 for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon. It checks whether a public JavaScript or TypeScript repo's README matches its code, sorting every checkable line into four buckets: Contradicted, Missing, Unverifiable, and Verified.

The core rule of the build is that models never decide what is true:

Job Who does it
Split the README into lines and settle obvious headings/badges Deterministic code rules
Label what kind of claim a prose line makes (command, dependency, env var, file/URL) Jev (jev-1.13.0) via Glasser, gated at 0.8 confidence
Decide Verified, Contradicted, or Missing Five deterministic code verifiers
Write a two-sentence plain-English summary from the counts Claude Haiku (claude-haiku-5-5), fail-open

When you wire that many moving parts together (AdaL, Jev, Glasser, Haiku, GitHub, and Vercel) and come back a month later to a red SCAN FAILED banner, it is hard to tell at first glance which piece broke.

Here is what was actually wrong, and the two fixes that came out of it.

1. When "javascript" hides "ava": @mansio's PR #2

Before I even got to the deployment keys, Mikhail (@mansio) had opened and landed PR #2, the project's first external code contribution.

Mikhail was testing README Clew 2 against real repositories and noticed something strange on sindresorhus/yocto-queue. The repo uses ava as a test runner, and the README never mentions ava. The coverage verifier should have flagged ava in the Missing bucket. Instead, it stayed silent.

Why? Because the README contained a link to Mozilla's documentation:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols

And inside the word javascript, in lowercase, sits the three-letter substring ava.

Our coverage check was using a plain substring match:

// Before: any substring match counted as "mentioned in the README"
if (readme.includes(name.toLowerCase())) continue;

Even worse, the same substring check lived in the dependency verifier's prose guard (inCodeContext), which checks whether a candidate package name appears on an install line. A short name like can inside npm i canvas-parser or lodash inside npm i lodash-es could bypass the prose guard and reach Contradicted, the exact false positive the guard was built to prevent.

The fix

Mikhail replaced both substring checks with a single whole-token rule, mentionsWord(), bounded by npm's own package name characters (A-Za-z0-9_-) plus @ and /:

export function mentionsWord(text, name) {
  if (!name) return false;
  const esc = name.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
  return new RegExp(`(?<![A-Za-z0-9_@/-])${esc}(?![A-Za-z0-9_-])`, 'i').test(text);
}

With that in place:

  • We use ava. and Tests run with \ava. still count as real mentions.
  • mozilla.org/.../javascript/... no longer hides ava.
  • npm i lodash-es no longer treats lodash as an installed package claim.

Mikhail shipped the fix with a 27-case test matrix and verifier controls in tests/mentions-word.test.js, matching the repo's file-size cap and offline test rules on the first try. If you have not read his engineering field notes on DEV (like The Dataset Was Lying: 4 of 6 "False" Facts Were True), go read him.

2. The 30-day time bomb: sending an expired token to a public API

Once Mikhail's PR was merged, I still had a live site that refused to scan.

Every click on SCAN returned HTTP 502:

{"error":{"code":"github_forbidden","message":"GitHub returned HTTP 401"}}

The ironic part: README Clew 2 only scans public repositories. It makes 4 metadata calls to api.github.com per scan and fetches the files from raw.githubusercontent.com. You do not even need a GITHUB_TOKEN for low-volume public reads (GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated REST calls per hour per IP, or 15 full scans per hour).

During the October hackathon, I had added a 30-day GitHub Personal Access Token so repeated test scans wouldn't hit the unauthenticated rate limit. Thirty days passed, the token expired, and lib/github.js kept sending Authorization: Bearer <expired_token> on every request.

GitHub allows requests with no Authorization header, but immediately rejects requests carrying an expired Authorization header with 401 Bad credentials. Because step 1 threw a GithubError, the pipeline stopped before Jev or Haiku ever ran.

The 4-line fix

First, I removed the expired GITHUB_TOKEN from Vercel. Second, we hardened lib/github.js so that if an expired token is ever present in .env or server environment variables and GitHub answers 401, the client drops the authorization header from the shared headers object and retries unauthenticated:

if (res.status === 401 && headers?.authorization) {
  delete headers.authorization; // expired or bad token: public repos work without it
  return request(url, { fetchImpl, headers, as });
}

Because headers is shared across the 4 metadata calls in fetchRepo(), dropping headers.authorization on the first 401 means the remaining 3 calls go straight out without the bad token.

3. Silent fail-open + Vercel environment scopes

The last piece was Claude Haiku. By design, Haiku is fail-open in README Clew 2: if the summary call fails or times out, the report still renders in full and the clew mascot falls back to a fixed one-line summary per mood.

My October Anthropic key had also been rotated. When I added the new ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in Vercel, two classic traps bit me at the same time:

  1. The new key was scoped to Development in Vercel, while Production and Preview still held the 34-day-old key.
  2. Vercel environment variable changes only take effect on the next deployment.

Running vercel env ls made the split visible right away:

Variable Environment Created
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (new) Development Today
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (old) Production, Preview 34d ago
GLASSER_API_KEY Production, Preview, Development 34d ago

Overriding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY across all three environments (Production, Preview, Development) and running vercel --prod brought the Haiku summary and bucket notes back on the first scan. Meanwhile, Glasser and Jev (jev-1.13.0) never missed a beat: all 4 batched calls completed in 1.37 seconds for about half a cent ($0.0055), with $10.80 of the original hackathon balance still untouched.

Related reading on DEV

Two posts from the community hit the exact operational edges from today's debugging session:

  • ["Invalid API key" or undefined env vars on Vercel: how to fix it] by @unbreakkit walks through how environment variable scopes (Production vs Preview vs Development) and missing redeploys cause 401 Invalid API key errors on Vercel even after you paste a fresh key.
  • [Your AI Agent Runs for Hours. Its GitHub Token Might Not.] by @__be2942592 looks at what happens when code assumes a GitHub token in the environment is valid forever instead of handling 401 expiration explicitly.

Try it

  • Live page: readme-clew-2.vercel.app (click USE DEMO REPO, then SCAN)
  • Source and 478 offline tests: github.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2

Thank you again to Mikhail (@mansio) for finding the substring bug on a real repo and shipping a clean, well-tested fix.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect. That is the lens I am writing from.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: Shipping in-browser WASM background removal without crashing Safari tabs (+ an open real-device latency dataset)
articles.description: Over the past month I built and shipped remove.ac, an image background remover split into two...
articles.body_html:
Over the past month I built and shipped remove.ac, an image background remover split into two explicit execution paths: a free in-browser WebAssembly studio where image bytes stay inside the tab, and an optional stateless Cloud GPU API (POST /v1.0/removebg) compatible with remove.bg payloads.

Running a 1024px segmentation model (onnxruntime-web WASM + guided-filter hair refinement) inside real users' browsers surfaced a few bugs that never showed up on an M-series MacBook during development. Here is what broke, how we fixed it, and the raw telemetry we collected from 2,000+ production runs.

1. WebKit holds onto offscreen <canvas> memory after unmount

Dropping references to temporary <canvas> elements in React was enough in Chromium, but iOS and macOS Safari kept hundreds of megabytes of backing-store memory pinned across batch runs. Explicitly zeroing dimensions (canvas.width = 0; canvas.height = 0) in teardown routines reclaimed memory immediately and stopped mobile tab reloads during 50-image ZIP batches on /batch.

2. Bounding manual brush undo history to 64 MB

On a 12 MP product photo, storing 10 undo snapshots as raw RGBA ImageData eats ~480 MB on its own. For the local Erase / Restore / Smart Brush and point/box subject selector, we switched to replaying stroke vectors on top of a rolling checkpoint canvas, capping undo history at 12 steps within a 64 MB ceiling.

3. Never silently fall back from local WASM to a backend server

A subtle trust bug in "hybrid" web tools is catching an out-of-memory WASM error and quietly uploading the file to a cloud worker so the task succeeds. If someone picked on-device processing for an ID scan or unreleased product shot, silent fallback violates the whole point. On remove.ac, local failures stay local; Cloud GPU runs only when a signed-in user clicks it or calls the API with an X-Api-Key (rac_live_...).

4. Bypassing serverless ~4 MB gateway caps without storing user files on S3

Standard serverless HTTP gateways choke around 4.5 MB, which fails as soon as a studio photographer outputs a 15 MB lossless PNG. Instead of staging uploads in an object bucket, our zero-dependency SDKs and CLI request a single-use HMAC ticket from POST /v1.0/removebg/ticket (placing a Postgres FEFO credit hold) and stream up to 25 MB / 40 MP directly into volatile GPU worker RAM. If inference errors out or times out, the credit hold releases automatically at zero cost.

Open SDKs (MIT) and Real-Device Latency Dataset (CC BY 4.0)

  • Zero-dependency Node.js & Python SDKs + --watch folder CLI: github.com/szp2005/remove-ac-sdk (includes a 1-line from removebg import RemoveBg drop-in shim).
  • Rolling 90-day real-device WASM benchmark dataset: remove.ac/benchmarks — publishes p50/p95 download, session-init, and inference timings across desktop/mobile CPU buckets (raw JSON and CSV under CC BY 4.0, no cherry-picked single-machine numbers).

If you want to poke at the browser WASM studio (no login wall) or test /v1.0/removebg with the free signup credit, everything is live at https://remove.ac. Happy to share details on the guided-filter worker pipeline or the Postgres FEFO ledger SQL!

articles.title: I built a racing sim that runs in a browser tab
articles.description: im racing usually starts with a big download and a decent PC. I wanted one you could open from a...
articles.body_html:
im racing usually starts with a big download and a decent PC. I wanted one you could open from a link.

That's LibreCorsa. It runs in the browser and it's open source. There are 2026-style open-wheelers, GT3s, a prototype and a road car, more than a dozen circuits, AI races, ghosts, rain and online races. You can drive it with a keyboard, a gamepad, a touch screen or a steering wheel. If you'd rather watch first, there's a 40-second trailer.

I'm building it on my own. It's a little over 800 commits since mid-October, and a few parts turned out much more interesting than I expected.

500 Hz, whatever your screen does

If the physics depends on frame rate, a 144 Hz monitor gives you more grip than a 60 Hz laptop. In a racing game you notice that within a lap.

So the simulation moves in fixed 2 ms steps (500 Hz), and each step splits into four 0.5 ms substeps for the tyres and suspension. The screen renders at whatever rate it can, and the sim catches up in whole steps. Stripped down, it's the classic loop:

const STEP = 0.002; // 500 Hz
let acc = 0;

function frame(dt: number) {
  acc = Math.min(acc + dt, 0.1); // a long hitch doesn't turn into a death spiral
  while (acc >= STEP) {
    sim.step(STEP); // four 0.5 ms substeps inside
    acc -= STEP;
  }
  render(sim.state);
}

One detail I didn't see coming: your steering input arrives once per frame, but a frame can run three physics steps or none. So each change is spread across the steps that frame actually runs, the way a real wheel turns, instead of landing all at once on the first one.

Does it hold? I run the same three-second launch at 30, 60, 144 and 240 fps, and the car ends within 0.3 km/h and 0.2 m every time. The test suite runs it at two frame rates and fails if they disagree.

Tyres are most of the work

The tyre is a Pacejka-style slip curve with combined slip, load sensitivity and carcass relaxation. Then it gets complicated. Each tyre tracks inner, middle and outer temperatures, and those move the grip window. Pressure follows the ideal gas law and changes how stiff the carcass is. Tyres wear. In the rain the road carries a water film that builds and drains, the cars dry the racing line first, and wets clear water up to a depth before they aquaplane.

The ground under the tyre mattered more than I thought. With one ground sample per wheel, a kerb's step edge gets hit at a point instead of rolled over. Each tyre now takes five samples across its contact patch (centre, both ends, both edges) and folds them into one height and slope.

There are two vehicle models. The default car has a planar chassis with sprung heave, pitch and roll. The others run a full 6-DOF rigid body with suspension built from hardpoints, so camber, bump steer and anti-dive come out of the geometry instead of numbers I typed in. On those cars the steering torque is the front tyres' moment about the kingpin axes. That's what a wheel actually pushes back with.

Checking it against a real car

When you're the only tester, tuning by feel only goes so far. I have about 24 minutes of MoTeC logs from a real GT3 Evo at Valencia, so the sim's GT3 runs the same manoeuvres: sustained cornering, braking and full-throttle acceleration at each speed, plus the gearing and the understeer gradient.

Right now every point sits within −13 % to +17 % of the logs. Not great, not terrible. The validation page is generated from the sim's own code with one command, and it has a section for where the sim is wrong. CI fails the build if a point leaves its band, and the last physics rework pushed one of them out.

Steering wheels in a browser

Steering, pedals and buttons were the easy part. If your OS sees the wheel as a game controller, the Gamepad API sees it too.

Force feedback is not easy. Chrome and Edge have WebHID, so a page can talk to a wheel base directly, and bases that speak the standard USB HID PID force-feedback reports can be driven with nothing installed. Plenty of popular wheels don't speak it. Logitech's force feedback is proprietary, for one. For those there's a small Windows helper that talks DirectInput and listens on localhost.

Where it stands: the one wheel I've tested, a MOZA R9, connects and steers over WebHID, but I haven't confirmed force feedback on it yet. It's marked experimental. If you have a different wheel, there's a wheel report form on GitHub and I'd love to see it filled in.

Racing people without paying for servers

Multiplayer is peer-to-peer over WebRTC. You host a room and send the link, or a friend types a 6-character code. If you want zero servers, there's a manual offer/answer copy-paste with nothing in between. Two tabs on the same machine can also race each other, which made testing a lot less lonely.

On the live site a small Cloudflare Worker does the rest. It pairs players, hands out relay servers for networks that block a direct link, keeps the leaderboards, and starts an open race every 20 minutes on the week's circuit and car. If nobody shows up, you race the AI.

Half a gigabyte, hosted for free

The game is a static Next.js export on Cloudflare, which is great until a circuit model is bigger than the asset store's 25 MiB per-file limit. Those files sit in an R2 bucket instead. The Worker answers any path that has no static file from R2, at the same URL, so the game never knows.

Car models are meshopt-compressed when the site builds. The default car drops from 16 MB to 6 MB, which matters when the first thing a player sees is a loading screen.

Hosting costs nothing at the moment. I'd like to keep it that way.

Licences, and why the repo is small

The code is MIT. The 3D models and sounds come from a lot of different authors with their own licences, and some are non-commercial. So LibreCorsa has no ads and nothing for sale. There's a Buy Me a Coffee link and that's it.

It's also why the repository carries only one circuit, RISE Motordrome, and the 2026 prototype car. Everything else is served on the site for playing there. A clone still gives you a working game with those two, and there's a guide for porting your own cars locally.

What's rough

VR works through WebXR, but it's a work in progress. Force feedback in the browser is experimental. Circuits converted from community 3D models have less trustworthy surfaces than the hand-built ones. And the handling is tuned by one person, which is exactly why I want other people driving it.

Try it

It's at librecorsa.org, and the code is on GitHub. Tell me how it drives, especially on a gamepad or a wheel I don't have, and how it runs on your machine.

LibreCorsa is an independent fan project. It isn't affiliated with Formula 1, the FIA, or any team or circuit.

articles.title: Compressing and resizing GIFs entirely in the browser
articles.description: Compressing and resizing GIFs entirely in the browser   Chat apps still treat GIF as a...
articles.body_html:
Compressing and resizing GIFs entirely in the browser

Chat apps still treat GIF as a first-class attachment, and they still enforce hard upload limits. The usual fix is to send the file to an online compressor. That works, but it is a lot of trust for a bug-report clip or a meme you would rather keep on the device.

You do not need a server for this. Decode the palettized frames into RGBA, transform them, and encode again — with GIF's 10-millisecond delay precision — and the whole job can stay inside a browser tab.

Keep the UI thread out of it

The practical constraint is memory and main-thread jank, not network. Expanding a large, many-frame GIF into full canvases can allocate hundreds of megabytes. I run the work in a module Web Worker: the page posts a File, receives progress events, and gets back a Uint8Array that becomes an object URL.

On the way in, gifuct-js parses the file and I composite every frame onto a full-size canvas, honoring disposal 2 (clear the dirty rectangle) and disposal 3 (restore the saved canvas). After that, every frame is a complete RGBA buffer, which makes resize, crop, and frame-dropping straightforward.

Two guardrails matter on phones. First, I cap total pixels across all frames — 60 million in this pipeline, about 240 MB of RGBA — and, if a file is over budget, downscale while decoding. Second, I clamp frame delays to a 20 ms minimum. Many browsers, and clients such as Discord and Slack, treat a delay under 20 ms as 100 ms. Honor a file's 10 ms delays when speeding a clip up, and the export can play slower than you intended.

const MIN_SAFE_DELAY = 20; // shorter delays often play as 100 ms

function roundDelay(ms) {
  return Math.max(MIN_SAFE_DELAY, Math.round(ms / 10) * 10);
}

When a speed change would push a frame below that floor, I merge it into a neighbor and carry the leftover time.

Encoding only what changed

Encoding uses a vendored copy of gifenc: a per-frame palette of 2–256 colors, then LZW. Opaque animations get a useful extra step. After the first full frame, each later frame is compared against the pixels already on screen — the quantized result, not the pre-palette source, so rounding errors do not accumulate. Only the bounding box of changed pixels is written. Unchanged pixels inside that box are marked transparent so the previous frame shows through. If nothing changed at all, I write a 1×1 transparent pixel just to preserve the delay.

Animations that already contain transparency cannot use that trick safely. They are written as full frames with disposal 2, so holes stay holes even if the file grows. A diffTolerance lets nearby RGB values count as unchanged: 0 is lossless deduplication; higher values trade a little smearing for a smaller dirty rectangle.

Resize is not a single algorithm

Shrinking and enlarging need different filters. When the output is smaller or the same size, I use area averaging with premultiplied alpha so thin transparent edges do not go muddy. When enlarging, I use bilinear sampling. A square crop is a centered cut with no movable box — fine for avatars, easy to clip a waving hand if you skip the loop preview. Changing dimensions does not guarantee a smaller file, which is why a compressor and a resizer should be different tools: one asks for a width (128–800 px presets, or an exact size up to 4,000 px), the other asks for a byte target.

A ladder, not a single knob

To aim at 512 KiB or 1 MiB, I do not expose a vague “quality 70.” I walk a fixed ladder and stop at the first encode that fits: fewer colors (256 down to 32), a smaller scale (100% down to 30%), then fewer frames (keep every frame, then every second, third, or fourth), while also raising the inter-frame tolerance. Dropped frames donate their delay to the frame that is kept, so the decoded duration stays the same even if the motion gets choppier.

If no step fits, the tool returns the smallest candidate and says so. A 30%-wide, 32-color, every-fourth-frame export of a long, grainy clip can still miss a 256 KiB budget. Trim the clip or resize to the display size first — smaller dimensions usually look better than heavier color reduction. Flat colors also compress far better than film grain or camera shake.

The same worker converts WebP. Still images go through createImageBitmap. Animated WebP needs the ImageDecoder API so every frame is recovered; I also inspect the RIFF chunks for ANIM / ANMF (or the VP8X animation flag). If the file is animated and the browser cannot decode frames, conversion stops rather than exporting only the first frame.

If the destination accepts MP4, compare a video export as well. Google's notes on replacing GIFs with video are a good reminder that GIF is a convenience format, not a compression format.

I wired this pipeline into the free browser tools on ImageToGif, including a GIF compressor that aims at a size you choose. The file never leaves the tab, there is no account, and nothing adds a watermark. I would like to hear if you have hit a 10 ms delay that plays as 100 ms.

articles.title: I put twelve 3D guests on our wedding website instead of writing "smart casual" (no 3D library)
articles.description: Shani and I get married in March 2027, in the highlands of South Africa. Every wedding website I...
articles.body_html:
Shani and I get married in March 2027, in the highlands of South Africa. Every wedding website I looked at had the same dress-code section: a line that says "smart casual" and leaves everyone guessing.

So I built ours by hand, and on the "What to wear" page I put twelve guests instead of a sentence.

boomslangchips.github.io

They show what to wear on each day of the weekend. They breathe, shift their weight, look around, fold their arms, glance at each other. You can drag one to turn them round, tap to step closer, and try the wedding colours on them.

There is no game engine and no 3D library behind it: about 250 KB of plain JavaScript and WebGL 1, plus one 760 KB file for the bodies. It runs on a phone.

How it fits together

File What it does
atelier-core.js Vectors, matrices, mesh building (tubes, shells, patches) and the WebGL renderer: skin, cloth, knit, denim, satin and hair shaders, a soft shadow map, the floor's reflection
atelier-body.js Reads the MakeHuman base mesh (CC0) in three body shapes, 163 bones and skin weights, and poses a body
atelier-cloth.js A small position-based cloth simulation for skirts and long hair, kept out of the body by the body's own cross-sections
atelier-figure.js One guest: body, face, hair, every garment cut round that body, shoes, accessories, and the arm poses
atelier-stage.js The stage: day tabs, dragging, the colour swatches, and each guest's little "mind" (breath, weight shifts, glances, blinks, smiles)

The hardest part was hands

Rendering was not the hard bit. Hands were.

A hand "on the hip" that floats a centimetre away looks wrong instantly. One that sinks into the hip looks worse. Folded hands that pass through each other are the first thing anyone notices. So each resting pose is solved: two-bone IK for the arm, then a small solver that places the palm against the surface it rests on, for every body shape.

The stage also watches its own frame time and does less on slow devices, and nothing moves at all if you have reduced motion turned on.

Honest limits

  • The guests stand in place: no walking.
  • Fingers keep one relaxed shape.
  • Creases at elbows and knees are drawn on the cloth, not simulated.
  • All faces are variations of one head.

The rest of the site

Our real site is private (it has our guest list on it), so I made a twin with a made-up couple and stock photos that you can click through: the invitation gate, a countdown, the weekend day by day, a drawn venue map, where to stay, an RSVP that knows who is on each invitation, and add-to-calendar.

👉 Demo: https://demo.wentzel.wedding (the invitation code is DEMO)
👉 3D guests, MIT licence: https://github.com/BoomslangChips/wedding-guests-3d

I wrote it with Claude Code over a few very long days. Happy to answer how any part works in the comments.

articles.title: Vercel UI SDK Beta, Hands On: 91 Behaviors, 4-Second Install, 36 KB per Popup
articles.description: Vercel's UI SDK went into public beta at 01:12 this morning, and by breakfast I had it installed,...
articles.body_html:
Vercel's UI SDK went into public beta at 01:12 this morning, and by breakfast I had it installed, counted, and running. Four seconds to install. Zero dependencies. Ninety-one behaviors, not the "50+" on the tin. And the first one I tried, a popover, opened, took focus, closed on Escape, and handed focus back, exactly as the docs promised.

That last part is the one I did not expect. First-day betas usually have a gap between the docs and the download. This one, on the one behavior I ran, did not.

Install: 4 seconds, nothing attached 

added 1 package in 4s

One package, no dependencies of its own, 7.5 MB on disk. The distribution folder holds 388 JavaScript files totalling 2.1 MB, plus docs and a skills folder that ship inside the package itself. The main entry point is a 7 KB barrel file; the real code lives in the subfolders. License is Apache 2.0, version 0.1.0-beta.1.

The docs deserve a line of their own. The package carries an 8,027-line llms.txt plus a full core.md guide, and a skills folder with reference pages for building components, patterns, styles, and testing. The pitch is that agents assemble interfaces from these behaviors, and the docs are packaged to be read by the thing doing the assembling. Whether that pitch lands is a question for a longer test. The packaging itself is deliberate.

The count: 91 behaviors, and what that number means

The announcement says 50+ interaction behaviors. I counted every create* function exported across all 70 subpath entry points, plus the main entry. The total is 91 distinct functions, and every single subpath loaded without an error.

But 91 needs a footnote, because two different kinds of thing are hiding in it. The main entry exports 36 low-level behaviors: createPopup, createSelection, createTypeahead, createRovingFocus, createVirtualizer, createUndoStack, and 30 more of that kind. The other 55 are component controllers, one per widget, with names like createTabsController, createCalendarController, and createDatePickerController. Both are real, both are usable, but they are not the same kind of building block. If you were hoping for 91 low-level behaviors, the honest count is 36. If you count controllers, 91 is fair, and the "50+" claim holds either way you slice it.

What I measured Result
Install time 4.3 s
Dependencies 0
Size on disk 7.5 MB (6.6 MB dist, 388 files)
Subpath entry points 70
create* functions, total 91
Low-level behaviors (main entry) 36
Component controllers 55
One popover, bundled + minified 98 KB (36 KB gzipped)
Whole main entry, bundled + minified 190 KB (71 KB gzipped)

The run: one popover, start to finish

I built the docs' own example, an invite popover, from the "A Popup of Your Own" page: popupState for state, createPopup with the popover preset for behavior, and the slot builders for the trigger, the content, and the close button. Then I drove it in a simulated DOM: click the trigger, press Escape, open it again, close it with the Done button.

mounted in 60 ms
1. initial state.open = false | mounted = false
   trigger aria-expanded = false
   content present in DOM = false | hidden attr = true
2. after clicking Invite: state.open = true | mounted = true
   trigger aria-expanded = true
   content data-side = top
   activeElement is inside content = true
   last change: {"key":"open","value":true,"reason":"trigger-press","source":"mouse","label":"Invite"}
3. after Escape: state.open = false | mounted = false
   focus returned to trigger = true
   last change: {"key":"open","value":false,"reason":"escape-key","source":"keyboard","label":"Invite"}
4. reopened: state.open = true
   after clicking Done: state.open = false | focus back on trigger = true
total changes recorded: 4
unmounted cleanly. total run time: 497 ms

Every step did what the docs said it would. The trigger carries aria-haspopup="dialog" and flips aria-expanded. The content gets role="dialog", aria-labelledby pointing at the trigger, and popover="manual", and the positioning engine computed real placement values, including which side of the trigger the popup landed on. The change log records not just what happened but why and how: trigger-press from the mouse, escape-key from the keyboard. Focus moved into the popup on open and came back to the trigger on close, both times, which is the part of popup behavior that usually breaks first.

This is what the rendered markup looked like after the run, trigger first:

<button data-slot="invite-trigger" id="mount-1-trigger" aria-haspopup="dialog"
  aria-expanded="false" type="button" data-closed="">Invite</button>

<div data-slot="invite-content" role="dialog" id="mount-1-content" tabindex="-1"
  aria-labelledby="mount-1-trigger" data-presentation="popover" popover="manual"
  style="position: fixed; inset: -4px auto auto 8px; margin: 0px;
  --available-height: 0px; --available-width: 0px; --anchor-width: 200px;
  --anchor-height: 40px; --transform-origin: 92px 0px; --arrow-offset: 6px;
  z-index: 2147483000;"
  data-side="top" data-align="center" data-closed="" hidden="">

The styling hooks are all there as data attributes and CSS variables: side, alignment, anchor size, transform origin, arrow offset. Nothing is styled for you; the parts arrive unstyled and you bring your own CSS. That is the design, not an omission, and the docs say so plainly.

One more thing the run confirmed: the same createPopup call changes character entirely when you swap the preset. The docs list four, popover, dialog, tooltip, and hover card, each choosing the content's role, how it opens and closes, and whether it is modal. I only ran the popover preset, so the other three are untested by me, but the mechanism is a single option, not a different behavior.

The catch: one popup costs 98 KB

That is the number that made me pause. Bundling the single popover behavior with a minifier came to 98 KB, 36 KB gzipped. The whole main entry, all 36 behaviors, is 190 KB minified. So one popup pulls in about half the library, because the shared foundation, positioning, layers, focus handling, comes along with it.

Is 36 KB gzipped too much for a popup? Depends on the page. On a dashboard that already ships a component library, it is in the same league as what you are already paying. On a landing page where the popup is the only interactive thing, it is a lot. What I can say from the count is that the tree-shaking works, one behavior is half the library rather than all of it, but the floor is high because the foundation is heavy. That is the tradeoff of the design: the behaviors are genuinely shared, so the first one pays for the plumbing.

What I did not test

This ran in jsdom, a simulated page, not a real one. State, attributes, focus, and keyboard handling all work there, and the SDK's own testing kit documents jsdom as a valid way to drive a primitive. Paint, layout, and real pointer behavior are untested by this run. I ran one behavior out of 91, and one preset out of four. And this is beta.1, released hours ago: the count, the sizes, and the behavior are all a snapshot of this morning, and any of them can move.

Still, the first impression is unusually solid for a day-one beta. The install is clean, the "50+" claim undersells the count, the docs match the download, and the one behavior I ran behaved itself completely. The thing to watch is the bundle floor: 36 KB gzipped for a single popup is the price of admission, and it is worth knowing before you build on it.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: A $0 page builder for local shops: one form, two short keys, and a beacon that tells a reader from a link preview
articles.description: Six shop-link services priced over 36 months, then the engineering behind the free one: one form, an edit key instead of an account, and a 2 KB beacon that tells a reader from a link preview.
articles.body_html:
Every local shop I look at has the same hole. Five stars on Google Maps, a price list taped to the counter, and a "website" button on the listing that goes to a Facebook page last updated in 2022. About 17% to 43% of small businesses still have no site, depending on which survey you read, and plenty of the ones that do have a page that cannot answer "how much" and "are you open" without a tap.

I built the smallest thing that answers those two questions, and put the bottom tier at $0. This post is the engineering: what it is made of, what it costs to run, and the two design decisions I am still not sure about.

The business reason first, because it shaped the code

Six services a shop could use as its one bio link, priced over 36 months at each vendor's own annual rate, read in November 2026:

  • Linktree: Starter $7/mo = $252, Pro $14 = $504, Premium $30 = $1,080
  • Beacons: Free $0, Creator $100/yr = $300, Plus $300/yr = $900, Max $1,000/yr = $3,000
  • Wix: Light $17/mo = $612, Core $29 = $1,044, Business $39 = $1,404
  • Squarespace: Basic $19/mo = $684, Core $29 = $1,044, Plus $49 = $1,764
  • MapToSite: Card $0, Board $6.99/mo = $251.64, Sign $13.99/mo = $503.64

The entry tiers land inside a $430 band and the useful tiers inside a $500 one. Price does not separate these products, so I could not compete on price. The only honest differentiator left was what the page contains — which meant the page had to be cheap enough to give away and good enough to be worth the link.

The flow, end to end

  1. The hero input takes a Google Maps link (or a place name). POST /api/place resolves it to {name, industry, lat, lng, maps_url}. Only the URL and its redirect are read: the place name comes out of the address (/maps/place/<name>/@lat,lng), the industry from a word list (barber, cafe, food, beauty, hair, fitness...), and an unreadable link just falls back to typing the name. Google's page is not scraped and nothing is stored.
  2. /create is a two-step form: business type, then name, phone, hours and three prices. Picking an industry tab advances the step by itself, so the only decision on screen is the one being asked.
  3. Publish mints a slug, returns {ok, slug}, and the page renders at /s/{slug} — about 64 KB of HTML with no framework and no client bundle worth measuring.
  4. The edit key is the only credential. Paste it on /dashboard and the page opens for edits. No email, no password, no session, nothing to breach but a random string the owner was shown once.

No sign-up is an architecture choice, not a growth trick: the record is created by the request that needs it, and the key is the whole identity.

The beacon: telling a reader from a link preview

Attribution is one file, /assets/beacon.js — 2,156 bytes, 1.1 KB gzipped, no cookie, no id. It posts a short JSON body to /api/beacon with two-character keys (p path, r referrer, s/m/c/t UTM fields, e event, x viewport) so the payload stays under 2 KB, which is also the worker's own limit.

The worker writes one row into D1:

traffic_events(id, created_at, path, referrer, utm_source, utm_medium,
               utm_campaign, utm_content, ip_hash, event, meta, is_internal, internal_reason)

Three details in there are the whole analytics stack:

  • Same-site untagged moves are dropped. A view with no UTM whose referrer is our own origin is a page the visitor already counted, so "direct" does not inflate as people click around.
  • meta carries the product and the viewport (mt-m390 = MapToSite, 390px wide). One D1 database serves two products without a schema fork; the mt- prefix is the join condition.
  • Rows are marked rather than deleted. is_internal plus internal_reason (ops-ip, ops-cookie, burst, machine traffic) keeps the owner's own checks and bot traffic in the table but out of the numbers a human reads.

The burst rule came from data: four seconds, more than one distinct ip_hash on the same path. When a page is pasted into Facebook, Slack or iMessage, the preview renderer fetches it within seconds from several addresses — I measured 49 "visits" landing in three seconds from 2–6 IPs after one post. A human reading a link does not do that. The channel rank query becomes:

SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(utm_source, ''), 'direct') AS src, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM traffic_events
WHERE meta LIKE 'mt-%' AND event = 'view' AND is_internal = 0
  AND created_at >= ?1
GROUP BY src ORDER BY n DESC;

Two bugs worth writing down

Open-now in the wrong time zone. The badge was computed from the shop's typed hours against the server's clock, which is Korean. A café in New York read "Open now" at midnight. The fix stores an IANA zone at publish time (tz=America/New_York) and evaluates the hours in that zone; pages published before the fix keep their old behaviour until edited. tests/open_state.mjs is at 97 passing — the case that breaks naive string comparison is a shop that closes at 2am.

Selling features the free plan already had. The pricing page listed "visit stats", "CSV export" and "inbox" as paid; the free plan returned all three. The fix was not copy, it was a table generated from the feature gate itself, so the page cannot drift from the code again.

What it costs to run

Pages and Workers on the free tier, D1 on the free tier, Polar as merchant of record so no card data touches the site. At the current volume — single-digit daily visitors, no paying customers — the marginal cost of a published page rounds to zero. If that stops being true, the paid tiers already answer it: $6.99 removes the footer credit and adds a photo gallery and a notice line; $13.99 adds the owner's domain and a one-time build.

The two questions I cannot answer from the code

Does a $0 tier pay for itself? The free page carries a "Free page · MapToSite" footer line. That is marketing if the people who see it are shop owners and noise if they are not. The beacon cannot tell me that yet, because it counts visits, not who is visiting.

Is an edit key better than an account? Less friction, less to breach, and a random string a barber can lose — and I cannot recover it for him. Accounts exist because they make recovery someone else's job; giving that up is a real cost, not a feature.

The comparison pages name the vendor URL and the date each price was read: the Linktree one, and the same table for Beacons, Wix and Squarespace. The builder itself: maptosite-app.pages.dev/create.

I build MapToSite; the $0 tier in that table is mine.
